newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: World labour leaders leave Seoul under a cloud.
newsitem.headline: World labour leaders leave Seoul under a cloud.

text.p: Four world labour leaders were hustled out of South Korea on Thursday after deportation warnings by authorities angry at what they viewed as outside meddling in the country's labour strife.

The four had attracted intense local media coverage with visits to Seoul's Myongdong Cathederal where strike leaders are sheltering from arrest and by appearing on stage as star guests at worker rallies.

A British member of the team was due to report to the Organisation for Economic Coooeration and Development (OECD) on a new labour law that has sparked three weeks of strikes and government threats against union leaders.
The OECD, which South Korea officially joined last December, is holding a meeting on January 22 to review the law.
But a Labour Ministry official said Seoul's partners in the Paris-based club of rich nations were powerless to change the legislation.
The OECD and foreign labour groups have said the controversial law violates worker rights to freedom of expression by maintaining a ban on new union bodies until 2000.

Marcello Malentacchi, head of the International Metalworkers' Federation, said before leaving that a last-minute tour of Daewoo Group factories was cancelled after immigration police warned them not to meet any more trade union leaders.

"I think Daewoo management must have been warned that our visit could cause unfriendly action by the government," said Malentacchi, who has been sporting a headband inscribed with the Korean word "fight".
Yoo Byong-kwang, a director general at the Justice Ministry, said the four were verbally warned they had violated the law.

"But they took part in protests in Myongdong and a mass rally despite the warning so we had to deliver a formal letter saying they would be deported unless they stopped these activities," he told Reuters.

The other three who left on Thursday are John Evans, head of a union advisory committee to the OECD; Guy Ryder, director of the Geneva office of the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU); and Takashi Izumi, the IFCTU's Singapore-based representative.
The delegation arrived last Saturday.
Seoul is expected to put up a vigorous defence of the law at the OECD meeting.
It argues the bill, which allows companies to lay off workers, replace strikers and adopt flexible work hours, is needed to cut industrial costs and boost competitiveness.

"All the OECD can do is put peer pressure on us. Nothing more nothing less," said Shim Kyung-ho, an official at the Labour Ministry and one of five delegates scheduled to attend next Wednesday's meeting in Paris.
Shim, who said there seemed to be a "misunderstanding" over the law, added: "The law has been revised to best meet the international labour law standards."
OECD chief Donald Johnston said last week he was worried about the unrest and had reminded Seoul's envoy in Paris of the organisation's commitment to human rights.
Malentacchi said he had planned to leave on Friday, although the other three had been scheduled to fly out on Thursday.
"I wanted to visit Hyundai factories in Ulsan today, but I was afraid to cause trouble," he said.
The southeast city of Ulsan has been a focal point of opposition to the three-week old labour law.
The four had warned that South Korea's reputation would suffer if there was a crackdown on union leaders who are demanding the government repeal the law.
On Wednesday, International Labour Organisation head Michel Hansenne said in Geneva there could be no solution to South Korean worker unrest unless union freedom was respected.
The only legitimate union group is the Federation of Korean Trade Unions. The militant Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, whose leaders are evading arrest, is outlawed.
